video_title: Why Bitcoin and AI Stocks Could EXPLODE Higher
gist: Carson Group chief market strategist Ryan Detrick argues the late-October sell-off is seasonal and that record cash hoards, extreme short positioning, midterm-cycle history, improving breadth and 30%+ earnings growth set up a Q4 surge and continued bull market into next year, despite AI capex/CDS risks. Contrary to the title, Bitcoin is discussed only briefly (a ~1.5% portfolio allocation); the episode centers on equities, breadth and the Fed.

insights.claim: Ryan Detrick says weakness in the first ~3 weeks of October is historically normal and that October 28th has historically been the strongest day of the year, typically marking a late-October low before a rally.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Treat late-October drawdowns as seasonal buying windows rather than trend breaks.
insights.quote: historically the strongest day of the year is October 28th

insights.claim: Detrick cites extreme bearish positioning as a contrarian buy signal: hedge funds hold their most shorts in 5 years and recently had one of their worst days since the day after the 2011 US debt downgrade.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Crowded shorts raise the odds of a max-pain squeeze higher into year-end.
insights.quote: hedge funds have their most shorts in 5 years

insights.claim: Three-month rolling inflows into money market funds and cash-like ETFs are the largest ever, alongside heavy inverse-ETF volume; Detrick argues such cash surges historically coincide with market bottoms.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Record sidelined cash is potential fuel for a rally rather than a sign of danger.
insights.quote: when you have these major surges in money market and cash like ETFs, we'll take a wild guess, that usually is when the market tends to bottom

insights.claim: After a 10% S&P 500 gain in Q2, the fourth quarter has been higher 9 out of 9 times, and Q4 has been up 12 of the last 13 years; with the S&P roughly flat so far in Q4, Detrick expects a fourth-quarter surge.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Seasonal base rates favor being long equities into year-end.
insights.quote: The fourth quarter is never been lower higher like nine out of nine out of nine times

insights.claim: Pompliano's base case is weakness into the midterm election followed by year-end strength once election certainty arrives, regardless of which party wins; Detrick agrees.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Position for post-election relief rally rather than trying to call the winner.
insights.quote: Once we get that certainty, we have strength going in through the end of the year.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 has been higher one year after each of the last 19 midterm elections, averaging roughly 15% gains, nearly twice the average any-time one-year return.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Post-midterm 12-month windows have a near-perfect positive track record.
insights.quote: S&P 500 has never been lower the last 19 times. 19 times a year later we're higher after midterms.

insights.claim: Detrick expects Democrats to likely retake the House while Republicans have a better chance of holding the Senate due to an easier map, producing a split Congress; the S&P 500 was up in each of the last 13 split-Congress years.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Gridlock historically has been equity-friendly, so a split outcome is not a bearish risk.
insights.quote: The last 13 years, Anthony, we had a split Congress, the S&P 500 was up.

insights.claim: Detrick sees healthy rotation beneath the surface: on down tech days 300-400 S&P stocks still rise, software rallied 6% last week, and healthcare and staples are 'ripping' while tech pauses.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Rotation, not tech alone, is sustaining the bull market.
insights.quote: Lifeblood Lifeblood of of bull is rotation.

insights.claim: Phil Rosen's chart showed that during the dot-com bust the S&P 500 fell almost 20% while the equal-weight S&P 500 rose 5.6%, illustrating that the average stock can rise while cap-weighted indices fall.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: A tech-led drawdown need not mean a broad bear market; equal-weight exposure can diversify.
insights.quote: the S&P 500 during the dot-com bust was down almost 20%. But if you take the equal weight S&P 500, it actually was up 5.6%

insights.claim: Jeff DeGraaf's (Renaissance Macro) buying-thrust signal fires when 55% of S&P 500 stocks hit 20-day highs; the S&P was higher a year later every time (~21-22 instances), last triggered in May 2025 after the Liberation Day sell-off.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Watch for the 55% 20-day-high threshold as a high-probability bullish confirmation.
insights.quote: When 55%of all the stocks in the S&P 500 hit a 20-day highs

insights.claim: Breadth improved markedly after October 1st with over 70% of stocks above their 20-day moving average; Detrick argues a tech rebound could push enough names to 20-day highs to trigger a new buying thrust.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Tech recovery is the missing ingredient to fire a buying-thrust signal.
insights.quote: over 70%of the stocks are above their 20-day moving average

insights.claim: The bull market just turned four; per Detrick no bull market in the last 50 years that reached its fourth birthday died before its fifth, and bull markets average 8 years.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Bull market age argues for at least another year of upside.
insights.quote: No bull market that made it to its fourth birthday last 50 years died before the fifth birthday.

themes.theme: AI/tech trade: valuations vs capex risk

insights.claim: S&P 500 valuation multiples are down roughly 15% this year while the index is up ~12-13% because earnings have grown over 30%, and Detrick expects multiple expansion next year on top of continued earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Earnings, not multiples, drove gains; re-rating would be an additional upside lever.
insights.quote: It's because earnings growth has grown over 30%this year

insights.claim: Detrick says Nvidia is as cheap as it has been in a long time and Amazon is as cheap as it has been as a public company, and expects tech to lead the market into next year.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Megacap tech pullback offers value entry points for the AI trade.
insights.quote: Amazon is as cheap as it's been since it's been a publicly traded company

insights.claim: The bear point Detrick concedes: credit default swaps on hyperscalers, Nvidia, Amazon and neoclouds are 'really blowing out' amid AI capex he says exceeds 1860s railroads, 1950s highways, the space race and the 1990s internet boom.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: AI capex financing stress is the key risk to monitor in credit markets.
insights.quote: The credit default swaps on a lot of these hyperscalers, Nvidia, Amazon, obviously some of the neo clouds. I mean, those are really, really blowing out.

insights.claim: Meta reported strong results but negative cash flow and fell 7-8%, after plans to raise about $90 billion for data centers, illustrating market sensitivity to AI capex burn.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Investors are now penalizing AI spenders whose free cash flow turns negative.
insights.quote: Then you look, it's like, "Ah, negative cash flow."

insights.claim: Carson Investment Research (~$9.1B managed) runs a slight tech overweight via XLK plus tactical semiconductor, software and high-momentum exposure, but avoids concentrated neocloud bets; momentum's 3-year excess return still sits in the 95th percentile even after its recent crash.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Broad ETF overweight beats narrow AI picks for risk-managed exposure.

insights.claim: About 15% of S&P 500 companies had reported with 88% beating EPS estimates, per Pompliano, and banks reported a solid consumer with ongoing lending and spending.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Earnings strength supports higher prices regardless of macro noise.

insights.claim: Forward 12-month earnings for small and mid caps are rising sharply, and Europe and emerging markets (led by South Korea's AI memory chip trade) show solid earnings, making this a global earnings-led bull market rather than a 'Magnificent Seven' story.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Diversify globally and down the cap spectrum to capture broad earnings growth.
insights.quote: this is a global bull market being led by global earnings, not just US large cap. It's not just seven stocks anymore.

insights.claim: The recreation products group was the best of ~110 sectors two weeks ago (+15%) then gained another ~8%, with POOL up 20% in October, signaling rotation into rate-sensitive consumer areas like housing.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Rebounds in beaten-down consumer groups are a leading indicator of economic strength.

insights.claim: Restaurant and bar retail sales have run at a 10-11% annualized pace over the last three months, which Detrick cites as evidence the consumer is not dead and the economy will stay strong into next year.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Discretionary spending contradicts the consumer-recession narrative.
insights.quote: The last 3 months, um restaurants are running at annualized like 10 or 11%.

insights.claim: Markets sold off on each of Fed Chair Warsh's first three meeting days; Detrick thinks the Fed is dovish at heart, sees one more hike in December and then a pause, contrary to major hawkishness priced in, noting 1997's one-and-done hike preceded a 30%+ market gain.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: If the Fed pauses after one more hike, hawkish pricing unwinds favorably for equities.
insights.quote: Maybe they do one more hike in um in December, and then we think they're probably going to take a break.

insights.claim: Detrick predicts the 10-year Treasury yield will be around 6% a year from now with stocks still higher, citing 6-8% nominal GDP growth and heavy corporate debt issuance; the late 1990s averaged a 6% 10-year with lower nominal growth.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Expect bonds to underperform; gradually rising yields can coexist with a bull market.
insights.quote: I wouldn't be shocked this time we come back in a year, this bull market's turning five, we're still higher, things are still hanging in there, and the 10-year yield's probably around 6%.

insights.claim: Detrick argues gradually rising yields are a net tailwind reflecting global growth, but a rapid jump in the 10-year to ~5.5% would cause destabilizing volatility.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: The speed, not the level, of yield moves is the equity risk.
insights.quote: if the 10-year yield went from here to 550 in a hurry, yeah, that's a lot of volatility, that'd upset the apple cart

insights.claim: Carson's unconstrained tactical models are ~68% equities, with the remaining 32% including ~1.5% Bitcoin, ~3% gold (first added in March 2023 during the regional bank crisis) and other real assets used in place of fixed income; Detrick's theme is 'diversify your diversifiers' as the Barclays Agg is still down for the year.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Hard assets replace part of bond allocations when yields stay stubbornly high.
insights.quote: Diversify your diversifiers is a theme we've said for a long time.

insights.claim: Carson has looked at but not adopted Bitcoin-backed perpetual preferreds from Strategy and Strive, citing compliance and need for more research.
insights.speaker: Ryan Detrick
insights.so_what: Institutional adoption of digital-credit yield products is still gated by compliance.
